title: Teaching Agents
summary: How to teach an AI agent a domain, and prove it learned. An agent's weights do not change in a session; it learns only through what enters its context and what is written down for the next one. The threshold is the cold-start test: knowledge counts only if a fresh agent, given the notes and not the answers, passes held-out checks.
sources: Brown et al.: Language Models are Few-Shot Learners (2020)
Liu et al.: Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts (2023)
Zheng et al.: Judging LLM-as-a-Judge with MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena (2023)

nodes.label: Context Is the Classroom
nodes.summary: Within a session an agent learns only through its context window: instructions, examples, tool results. Nothing else changes.
nodes.outcome: List exactly what an agent can know at a given step.
nodes.check: You correct an agent's mistake mid-session. What has changed in the model?
nodes.answer: Nothing in its weights; the correction exists only in this session's context.

nodes.label: "The agent will remember next time"
nodes.summary: Unless the lesson is written to durable memory, a skill or project instructions, the next session starts blank.
nodes.outcome: Persist a correction so a new session obeys it.
nodes.check: An agent apologises and promises not to repeat a mistake. What makes that promise true?
nodes.answer: Only writing the rule to persistent memory, a skill or instructions that load next time.

nodes.label: Outcomes as Specs
nodes.summary: State what the agent must be able to do as testable outcomes before writing any teaching material (backward design for agents).
nodes.outcome: Rewrite a vague instruction as outcomes with checks.
nodes.check: Rewrite 'be good at our codebase' as a testable outcome.
nodes.answer: E.g. 'given a bug report, locate the responsible module and write a failing test, unaided, on 4 of 5 held-out reports'.

nodes.label: Semantic Anchors
nodes.summary: Naming a well-known method ('Red/Green TDD', 'Pyramid Principle') loads its whole procedure from pre-training in two words.
nodes.outcome: Compress a procedure by replacing explanations with anchors, then verify behaviour is unchanged.
nodes.check: Why can 'use the Socratic Method' replace a paragraph of instructions?
nodes.answer: The model already knows the method from pre-training; the anchor activates it, so long as the term is precise and widely documented.

nodes.label: Worked Examples & Few-Shot
nodes.summary: A few input–output examples teach format and judgement better than abstract rules; vary them so the agent learns the pattern, not the instance.
nodes.outcome: Design a few-shot set that covers edge cases without being copied verbatim.
nodes.check: All three of your examples are short. What is the risk?
nodes.answer: The agent may infer that answers should be short; examples teach every regularity they share, intended or not.

nodes.label: Skill Files: Distilled Procedures
nodes.summary: Durable, loadable instructions (a SKILL.md) that turn a session's lessons into reusable procedure.
nodes.outcome: Distil a successful session into a skill with a contract, workflow and checks.
nodes.check: What separates a good skill from a long prompt?
nodes.answer: A contract (what must exist when done), a stepwise workflow, and verifiable checks, loaded only when relevant.

nodes.label: "More context always helps"
nodes.summary: Relevant facts buried in the middle of long contexts are used less reliably (Liu et al.); irrelevant material dilutes attention.
nodes.outcome: Trim a context and measure whether accuracy improves.
nodes.check: Where in a long context is a key fact least reliably used?
nodes.answer: In the middle (Lost in the Middle); start and end positions fare better.

nodes.label: Evals: Held-Out Checks
nodes.summary: Agent learning is measured only on checks it has not seen. This is the threshold: before it, 'the agent knows X' is a feeling; after it, it is a number.
nodes.outcome: Build a held-out eval set and report accuracy before and after teaching.
nodes.check: Why must eval questions never appear in the teaching material?
nodes.answer: Then the eval measures recall of the answer key, not learning (contamination).

nodes.label: The Cold-Start Test
nodes.summary: Spawn a fresh agent with only the distilled notes or skill, never the answers, and ask held-out checks. Pass means the knowledge transferred; fail locates the gap in the notes.
nodes.outcome: Run a cold-start test and revise the notes from its failures.
nodes.check: A tutor agent answers every check perfectly. Why is that not evidence the skill file works?
nodes.answer: The tutor has the whole session in context; only a fresh agent with just the skill shows whether the file carries the knowledge.

nodes.label: Answer-Key Hygiene
nodes.summary: Keep answers out of the learner agent's context: separate quiz prompts from answer keys, and grade with a different agent.
nodes.outcome: Generate quiz prompts without answers and grade in a separate context.
nodes.check: How does `dulta.py quiz` support answer-key hygiene?
nodes.answer: It prints checks without answers for the learner, and writes the key separately for the grader.

nodes.label: "An agent can grade its own answers"
nodes.summary: LLM judges favour their own outputs and the first option shown (self-preference and position bias, Zheng et al.). Grade with an independent judge and swap orders.
nodes.outcome: Set up an independent grader and control for position bias.
nodes.answer: Self-enhancement (favouring its own outputs) and position bias (favouring the first option); also verbosity bias.

nodes.label: Independent Critic Panels
nodes.summary: Several judges, each grounded in one authority and blind to the others, catch what a single reviewer misses.
nodes.outcome: Convene a panel with seats that disagree, each citing evidence.
nodes.check: Why should panel seats not see each other's verdicts in the same round?
nodes.answer: Independence: otherwise they anchor on the first verdict and errors correlate (wisdom of crowds needs independent judgements).

nodes.label: Tools as Procedural Knowledge
nodes.summary: Teaching an agent a tool means teaching when to call it, how to read its output, and how to verify it, not just its signature.
nodes.outcome: Write tool guidance with a when-to-use rule and a verification step.
nodes.check: An agent has a calculator tool but still does arithmetic in its head. What is missing from its teaching?
nodes.answer: A rule for when the tool must be used (e.g. any arithmetic beyond one step), with an example.

nodes.label: Durable Memory & Carry-Forward
nodes.summary: Facts established by evidence are written down once, indexed, and read at the start of the next session; stale entries are pruned.
nodes.outcome: Write a carry-forward entry with its evidence and verify it is loaded next session.
nodes.check: What should a carry-forward entry contain besides the fact?
nodes.answer: The evidence that established it and how it changes future behaviour.

nodes.label: Bounded Loops & Drift
nodes.summary: Long agent runs lose the goal or loop; caps, checkpoints and re-reading the contract keep them on track.
nodes.outcome: Add caps and a goal re-check to an iterative agent workflow.
nodes.check: A critic loop keeps raising the same objection. What should a bounded workflow do?
nodes.answer: Stop at the cap, log the objection as an open item, and ship the strongest version.

nodes.label: Agent Transfer
nodes.summary: The real test of an agent's learning: a task unlike the teaching examples, solved with the taught principles.
nodes.outcome: Design a transfer task and score an agent's attempt.
nodes.check: Why is an agent passing tasks that resemble its few-shot examples weak evidence?
nodes.answer: It may be pattern-matching the examples; only dissimilar tasks show the principle was learned.
